content: Carolina horsenettle, scientifically known as Solanum carolinense, is also referred to by various common names such as Bull nettle, Apple of Sodom, Radical Weed, Sand Brier, and Tread-softly. Despite its name, it is not a true nettle but belongs to the Solanaceae family, commonly known as the nightshade family. This plant is characterized by its painful spines along the stems, which can penetrate the skin and break off, causing irritation. Carolina horsenettle is a perennial, herbaceous plant native to the southeastern United States, but it has spread extensively across North America. Its leaves are alternately arranged, elliptic-oblong to oval in shape, and irregularly lobed or coarsely toothed. Both surfaces of the leaves are covered with fine hairs. The flowers of this plant have five petals and are typically white or purple with yellow centers, although a blue variant resembling tomato flowers also exists. The fruits of the plant resemble small tomatoes. When immature, the fruits are dark green with light green stripes, but they turn yellow and wrinkled as they mature. Each fruit contains approximately 60 seeds. The plant flowers throughout the summer, from April to October. All parts of the Carolina horsenettle are toxic. Cases of poisoning have been reported in children and cattle who consumed the green fruit. The mature fruit is considered to be either non-toxic or less toxic compared to the immature fruit. This plant is commonly found in pastures, roadsides, railroad margins, disturbed areas, and waste grounds. It typically grows to about 1 meter in height but is often shorter, existing as a subshrub. It thrives in sandy or loamy soils. Carolina horsenettle is classified as a noxious weed in several U.S. states. It can propagate both vegetatively through underground rhizomes and by seed. The plant is resistant to many herbicides, and herbicide use often inadvertently promotes its growth by eliminating competing weeds. Gardeners particularly dislike this weed because its spines can penetrate the skin and break off when the plant is handled. Additionally, its deep root system makes it challenging to remove. The plant is sometimes written as horsenettle, horse nettle, or horse-nettle, though USDA publications typically use horsenettle. Other common names for this plant include Wild tomato, Devil's tomato, and Sand Brier.
